transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I’m Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. Well, it's actually kind of embarrassing, to be honest. I'm a kindergarten teacher—I've been teaching for a while now since I got my degree—and you know, you'd think in my line of work I'd be completely used to everything a school environment throws at you. Kids, messes, chaos, loud noises, all of that is totally fine. I love my job, I really do. 

But... well, what brings me in today is something very specific that's been causing me a lot of trouble at work. It's... balloons. I know how silly that sounds for a kindergarten teacher, but the second I spot balloons at school—and I mean, even if they're all the way across the hallway, just tied to a cubby for a student's birthday party or something—my chest just instantly tightens up. It's this immediate, overwhelming physical reaction. I just completely freeze. I stand there, totally locked up for a moment, before I can even begin to think clearly about what I’m supposed to be doing or where I was leading my class. 

I mean, I have all these little kids relying on me to be in charge, and my body just reacts before my brain can even process it. I just stop dead in my tracks, and it takes me a minute to even remember what lesson I was supposed to be teaching. It's just so immediate and I can't seem to control it at all.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain places or events at school where you might see balloons, like birthday parties or decorations?

Oh, absolutely. I mean, I try to, as much as I possibly can. It’s actually gotten to the point where it’s changing how I run my classroom, which is really frustrating for me. 

Like with birthdays, for example. Birthdays are a huge deal in kindergarten, as you can imagine. The parents always want to bring in cupcakes or goody bags and, inevitably, they bring in those big bouquets of balloons. Lately, I’ve just been... well, I’ve been asking my classroom aides to handle the birthday circles entirely. I’ll make up an excuse, like I need to prep the next craft or catch up on some daily folders, and I just go to the other side of the room or step out into the hall. Bless my aides, they're wonderful, but I hate putting that on them. 

And it’s the same with school-wide events. We had a spring festival recently, and the PTA had these tables set up with balloons tied to every single chair, and I just... I couldn't do it. I had to keep moving away from the festival tables. I actually steered my entire line of kids to the complete opposite side of the courtyard just to avoid walking past them, which made us late for the music station. 

But the thing is, I can't *always* get away. Sometimes a parent walks right up to me at drop-off holding one, or I’m required to be at a specific spot for an assembly, and if I absolutely have to stay... I just try to keep as much physical distance between me and it as humanly possible. I'll stand way back, and I just focus all my energy on getting through the moment without looking at them. I’ll stare at my clipboard, or the kid’s shoes, or the floor—literally anything to not look directly at the balloons. I just sort of brace myself and wait for it to be over. It’s just so exhausting having to map out my entire day around where a piece of rubber might be.
When you see a balloon, does your reaction feel like a sudden surge of intense fear that peaks within minutes, like a panic attack?

Um... you know, I don't think so? I mean, I hear people talk about panic attacks, and my older sister actually had one once, years ago before her college finals, and she told me it felt like this massive wave that just kept building and building until she felt like she was having a heart attack and couldn't breathe. But for me, it's not really like a wave that builds up and peaks over a few minutes, if that makes sense. 

It’s more just... instantaneous. Like, boom, the balloon is there, and I’m just totally frozen. My chest gets super tight, like I mentioned before, and my muscles just lock up completely. It’s not this escalating terror where I feel like I'm losing my mind or gasping for air as the minutes tick by. It's just an immediate, rigid sort of dread. I just stand there holding my breath. 

Like, just last Tuesday, one of my kids, little Leo, walked into the morning circle holding this shiny, helium Spiderman balloon—and I didn't have a build-up of fear, I just instantly turned to stone the second the classroom door opened. I couldn't speak, I couldn't move toward him to greet him like I normally do, I just stared at the carpet. So, yeah, I wouldn't call it a surge that peaks, because honestly, the absolute worst part is the exact second I lay eyes on the thing. After that initial shock of seeing it, the fear doesn't really climb higher, I'm just incredibly tense and my brain is spinning, trying to figure out how to escape the situation without the kids noticing that their teacher is acting completely bizarre. I just stay in that locked-up, defensive mode until it's gone. So... no, I wouldn't say it's like a panic attack, at least not how I've heard them described.
When you're not at school or in situations where you might see balloons, do you find yourself worrying or thinking a lot about the possibility of running into them?

You know, it's funny you ask that, because... well, no, not really. I mean, when I'm at home, in my apartment, or, say, if I'm just running to the grocery store or getting coffee on a Sunday morning... I don't really think about balloons at all. It's not like this dark cloud hanging over my head every second of the day, if that makes sense. 

Like, I can sit on my couch and watch TV, or read a book, or prep my lesson plans for the week, and the thought of a balloon doesn't even cross my mind. I'm completely fine. I don't lay in bed at night tossing and turning, wondering if I'm going to see one the next day. It's really only when I'm actually in a situation where they are present, or when I'm walking into an environment where I *know* they might be—like the school on a Friday when I know there are three birthdays, or if I'm walking past a party supply store—that my radar goes up. But just sitting around in my normal, everyday life outside of those specific triggers? No, I'm not agonizing over it. I'm just living my life, totally oblivious to them until they actually pop up in my line of sight. It's almost like out of sight, out of mind, until it's very much in sight, and then my brain just short-circuits. So, no, I wouldn't say I worry about them constantly when I'm away from all that.
Have you ever had a physical reaction, like chest tightness or freezing up, to something that reminded you of balloons, like a picture of a balloon or even just thinking about them?

Um... no, not really. I mean, pictures don't bother me at all. Like, if I'm reading a storybook to the kids—because, you know, we read a lot of picture books in kindergarten, like *Curious George* or *Winnie the Pooh*, and there are always balloons in those—I don't have any physical reaction to seeing a drawing of one. It's just ink on a page, you know? It doesn't have that... that tight, rubbery look, or that awful squeaky sound when you rub against it, or that feeling that it's going to suddenly pop right in my face. It's flat. It's safe. 

And thinking about them... well, I mean, I'm talking to you about them right now, and I'm not freezing up or feeling my chest get tight. I'm definitely a little uncomfortable, just because it's not my favorite topic of conversation, obviously, but I'm not having that intense, locked-up reaction. It's really only the real, physical object that does it to me. The actual, inflated piece of rubber floating there in the room with me. 

Like, I can even go to the party store to buy decorations for my classroom—like streamers or those paper honeycomb things—and I can walk right past the aisle where they sell the uninflated balloons in those little plastic bags. Those don't bother me either, because they're just flat pieces of latex. They haven't been blown up yet. It's the inflation, the... the potential energy of it, I guess? The fact that it's this taut, stretched thing that could burst at any second. That's what gets me. So, no, pictures or just the concept of a balloon in my head, or even the uninflated ones in a package... they don't trigger that freezing feeling at all. It has to be the real thing, blown up and right there in front of me.
Has this reaction to balloons caused you any significant distress or affected your ability to function normally at work or in your personal life?

Well, yeah... I mean, that's really why I'm here, honestly. Because it's, it's definitely starting to bleed into my job, and that's the one thing I've always tried so hard to protect. I love teaching kindergarten, I really do. I've been doing it for seven years now, and I put so much of my heart into my classroom. But lately, it's just getting... complicated. 

Like, with the birthdays. You know, kids in kindergarten, birthdays are a massive deal. It's the highlight of their month. And parents always want to bring things in. I used to just sort of casually suggest they bring cupcakes or stickers, but now, if a parent walks in with a big bouquet of balloons, I completely freeze up. I've had to start making excuses to step out of the room. I'll grab my teaching aide, Sarah—who is wonderful, thank goodness—and I'll just sort of whisper to her, "Can you take over the birthday song? I need to run to the office," or "I forgot to make copies." And I'll literally hide in the staff workroom until I know the balloons are tied down somewhere or out of the room. Sarah has definitely noticed, and I feel so guilty putting that on her, because it's my classroom, you know? I should be the one leading the celebration. 

And then... well, there was this big spring festival we had a couple of weeks ago. I had spent weeks planning this huge, beautiful art table for the kids. We were going to make these giant tissue paper flowers, and I was so excited about it. But when I got there to set up, the PTA had decided to anchor the corners of my table with these massive, arching balloon columns. Just everywhere. And I... I just couldn't do it. I couldn't even walk up to my own table. I stood in the hallway for like ten minutes, trying to talk myself into it, but my chest was so tight I couldn't breathe right. I ended up having to text Sarah again and beg her to run the table, and I told my principal I had a sudden migraine and had to go home. 

And the thing is, my supervisor definitely noticed. She pulled me aside the following Monday and asked if everything was okay, because it was so unlike me to abandon a project I was that excited about. I just made up some excuse about feeling under the weather, but I could tell she was looking at me a little funny. I hate lying to her, and I hate that I missed out on seeing my kids do the art project I planned for them. So, yeah, it's definitely causing me distress, and it's absolutely getting in the way of my work. I just... I can't keep running out of my own classroom every time a piece of rubber floats through the door. It's exhausting.
Have you ever had a similar reaction to other objects that might resemble balloons, like beach balls, inflatable decorations, or even something like a round, red apple?

Well, no, not at all. It's really just the balloons. Like, an apple? Oh my gosh, no, definitely not an apple. I mean, we have snack time every day at 10:30 in my classroom, and half the kids bring apples or those little mandarin oranges, and it's totally fine. Because an apple is solid, you know? If you drop it, it just bruises, it doesn't explode. There's no tension there. 

And beach balls... it's funny you mention that, because we actually have a couple of those big, striped beach balls in the gym equipment closet at school. Sometimes when it's raining and we have to do indoor recess, I'll bring them out for the kids to bat around in the circle. And I'm completely fine with them. I think it's because... well, the plastic is so thick. It's that heavy vinyl material, you know? It doesn't have that awful, thin, stretched-out look that a balloon has where it looks like the rubber is just fighting to hold itself together. And even if a beach ball gets a hole in it or a kid steps on it, it just sort of sadly deflates, right? It just hisses and goes flat. It doesn't have that violent, sudden *bang* that just goes right through your chest. 

Even those huge inflatable decorations—like, you know the ones people put on their front lawns for Halloween or Christmas? The giant glowing snowmen or the big turkeys? My neighbor across the street, Dave, he puts up like six of them every December. It takes up his entire front yard, it's honestly a little ridiculous. But I can walk right past them while I'm walking my dog, or drive past them every morning, and I don't feel a thing. I mean, they're kind of loud because of the little air motors running to keep them blown up, but they don't scare me at all. 

So, yeah, it really is just... it's specifically balloons. If it's not a literal balloon, I don't have that reaction. I can handle pretty much anything else round or filled with air, as long as it's not that thin, rubbery latex. It's just that one specific thing that completely throws me off. Everything else is just everyday stuff to me.

My neighbor across the street, Dave, he puts up like six of them every December. It takes up his entire front yard, it's honestly a little ridiculous. But I can walk right past them while I'm walking my dog, or drive past them every morning, and I don't feel a thing. I mean, they're kind of loud because of the little air motors running to keep them blown up, but they don't scare me at all. 

So, yeah, it really is just... it's specifically balloons. If it's not a literal balloon, I don't have that reaction. I can handle pretty much anything else round or filled with air, as long as it's not that thin, rubbery latex. It's just that one specific thing that completely throws me off. Everything else is just everyday stuff to me.
